title: A required parameter cannot follow an optional parameter
meaning: An optional parameter comes before a required one.
cause: Callers can only leave off trailing arguments, so optional and defaulted parameters must come last. Reorder them, or take an options object.

title: Initializers are not allowed in ambient contexts
meaning: A `declare` statement gave a value.
cause: `declare` only describes something that exists elsewhere — it never creates it, so it cannot set a value. Drop the initializer, or drop `declare` if you meant to define it here.
bad: declare let version: string = "1.0";
good: declare let version: string;

title: The return type of an async function must be Promise<T>
meaning: An async function was annotated with a plain return type.
cause: An `async` function always returns a promise, whatever its body returns. Annotate what callers really get: `Promise<number>`, not `number`.

title: 'for await' loops are only allowed within async functions
meaning: A `for await` loop sits in an ordinary function.
cause: Waiting needs an async context. Make the enclosing function `async` (it then returns a promise), or move the loop to the module's top level.

title: Catch clause variable type annotation must be 'any' or 'unknown'
meaning: `catch (e: Error)` claims to know what was thrown.
cause: Anything can be thrown — a string, a number, `undefined` — so the compiler will not let you promise it is an `Error`. Leave it `unknown` and narrow with `instanceof Error`.

title: Decorators are not valid here
meaning: A decorator was put on something that cannot take one.
cause: Decorators apply to classes and class members only — not to plain functions or variables. For a function, wrap it in a higher-order function instead.

title: Unable to resolve signature of method decorator
meaning: The decorator's parameters do not match how decorators are called.
cause: Standard (TC39) decorators receive `(value, context)`. A legacy three-argument `(target, key, descriptor)` decorator only works under `experimentalDecorators`. Write the standard signature.

title: 'await' expressions are only allowed within async functions and at the top levels of modules
meaning: You used `await` inside a function that isn't `async`.
cause: Mark the enclosing function `async` (its return type becomes a `Promise`).

title: Type 'A' does not satisfy the expected type 'B'
meaning: A `satisfies` check failed.
cause: The expression before `satisfies` doesn't match the type after it. Note that for an object literal the compiler usually points at the offending property instead, as TS2322 — TS1360 is what you get when the whole value is wrong.
bad: const port = "8080" satisfies number;
good:
const port = 8080 satisfies number;
console.log(port);

title: Cannot be used as a value because it was imported using 'import type'
meaning: Something imported with `import type` was used at runtime.
cause: `import type` is erased completely, so nothing is there to call. Use a plain `import` for values; keep `import type` for names used only in types.

title: Duplicate identifier 'x'
meaning: Something is declared twice where only one declaration is allowed.
cause: Type aliases can't be reopened (interfaces can — that's declaration merging). Use one alias, or combine two with `&`.
bad:
type Point = { x: number };
type Point = { y: number };
good: type Point = { x: number; y: number };

title: Cannot find name 'x'
meaning: You used a name that isn't declared anywhere the compiler can see.
cause: A typo, a missing declaration, or a variable declared in a different scope (inside another block or function).
bad: console.log(totl);
good:
const total = 3;
console.log(total);

title: Module has no exported member
meaning: You imported a name the module does not export.
cause: Check the spelling and the module's actual exports — often a similarly named export exists (`readFileSync`, not `readFile`), or it is a default export.
bad: import { readFile } from "fs";
good:
import { readFileSync } from "fs";
console.log(typeof readFileSync);

title: Cannot find module
meaning: The import path does not lead to a module the compiler can see.
cause: Check the relative path and file name. For a package, its types must be installed. In a single-file program there is no `./math` — define it in the same file.
bad:
import { add } from "./math";
console.log(add(1, 2));

title: An interface can only extend an object type with statically known members
meaning: An interface tried to extend a union.
cause: An interface needs one fixed set of members to extend, and a union has several possible shapes. Use a type alias with an intersection instead.
bad:
type Pet = { name: string } | { id: number };
interface Owner extends Pet {}

title: Type 'A' is not assignable to type 'B'
meaning: You put a value somewhere whose declared type doesn't allow it.
cause: The most common error there is. Read it right to left: the thing on the right of the message is what the slot accepts; the thing on the left is what you tried to put in. Either the value is wrong, or the declared type is too narrow.
bad:
let count = 0;
count = "zero";
good:
let count = 0;
count = 0;

title: Property 'x' does not exist on type 'A'
meaning: You read a property the type doesn't have.
cause: Either a typo, or the value's type is wider than you think — e.g. a union where only one member has the property. Narrow first (`if ("x" in v)`, a tag check) or fix the name.

title: Property 'x' is private and only accessible within class 'C'
meaning: Code outside a class touched a `private` member.
cause: Go through a public method or getter instead. Note that `private` is compile-time only; `#x` is enforced at runtime too.

title: Type 'A' does not satisfy the constraint 'B'
meaning: A type argument doesn't meet its type parameter's constraint.
cause: Common with `Pick<T, K>` when `K` isn't a key of `T` — which is exactly the typo protection `Pick` gives you (and `Omit`, whose keys are unconstrained, doesn't).
bad:
type User = { name: string; age: number };
type Preview = Pick<User, "nmae">;
good:
type User = { name: string; age: number };
type Preview = Pick<User, "name">;

title: Argument of type 'A' is not assignable to parameter of type 'B'
meaning: A function was called with an argument its parameter doesn't accept.
cause: The same rule as TS2322, applied at a call. Check the argument's real type (hover it) against the parameter's declared type.

title: Value of type 'typeof X' is not callable. Did you mean to include 'new'?
meaning: A class was called like a function.
cause: Classes are constructed with `new`. Calling one without it throws at runtime, and TypeScript refuses it up front.

title: This expression is not callable
meaning: You called something that isn't a function.
cause: Often a property that's a value, not a method (`s.length()`), or a union where not every member is callable.
bad:
const word = "hi";
console.log(word.length());
good:
const word = "hi";
console.log(word.length);

title: Conversion of type 'A' to type 'B' may be a mistake
meaning: An `as` assertion between types that don't overlap enough.
cause: `as` never converts anything; it only makes a claim. For a real conversion call `Number(...)`, `String(...)` or a parser. (`as unknown as T` forces it — and makes the danger obvious.)
bad: const n = "5" as number;
good:
const n = Number("5");
console.log(n);

title: Object literal may only specify known properties
meaning: An object literal has a property its target type doesn't declare.
cause: This excess-property check applies only to fresh object literals, where an extra key is almost always a typo. Remove it, or add it to the type.
bad:
type Point = { x: number; y: number };
const p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2, label: "origin" };
good:
type Point = { x: number; y: number; label?: string };
const p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2, label: "origin" };

title: A function whose declared type is neither 'undefined', 'void', nor 'any' must return a value
meaning: A function with a declared return type never returns anything.
cause: Usually a forgotten `return` — often inside a braced arrow function, where the value of the last expression is not returned automatically.

title: The left-hand side of an arithmetic operation must be of type 'any', 'number', 'bigint' or an enum type
meaning: You did arithmetic (`-`, `*`, `/`, `%`) with a non-number on the left.
cause: JavaScript would coerce a string silently; TypeScript refuses. Convert with `Number(...)` first.
bad:
const input = "10";
console.log(input - 1);
good:
const input = "10";
console.log(Number(input) - 1);

title: Operator 'op' cannot be applied to types 'A' and 'B'
meaning: An operator was used between types it doesn't support.
cause: Often mixing `bigint` with `number`, or comparing values that can't be ordered. Convert one side so both match.
bad:
const big = 10n;
console.log(big + 1);
good:
const big = 10n;
console.log(big + 1n);

title: Function lacks ending return statement and return type does not include 'undefined'
meaning: Some path through a function falls off the end without returning.
cause: You declared a return type, but one branch doesn't return. Add the missing `return` — or, for a switch over a union, handle every member.

title: This comparison appears to be unintentional because the types 'A' and 'B' have no overlap
meaning: You compared two values that can never be equal.
cause: Usually a misspelled literal, or a value whose type was narrowed earlier so it can't be the thing you're checking for.

title: Duplicate function implementation
meaning: Two function bodies share a name.
cause: TypeScript allows several overload *signatures* but only one implementation. Rename one function, or merge them.
bad:
function area(w: number): number { return w * w; }
function area(w: number, h: number): number { return w * h; }
good: function area(w: number, h: number = w): number { return w * h; }

title: This overload signature is not compatible with its implementation signature
meaning: The implementation cannot handle every overload.
cause: The implementation signature must accept everything each overload accepts. Widen its parameter types (usually to a union) so every overload is covered.

title: Class incorrectly implements interface
meaning: A class says `implements X` but is missing some of X's members.
cause: `implements` is a checked promise: every member the interface lists must exist with a compatible type. Add what is missing (the message lists it).

title: Interface incorrectly extends interface
meaning: An extending interface redeclared a member with an incompatible type.
cause: A sub-interface may narrow an inherited member, never change it to something unrelated. Rename the new member, or rethink the relationship.

title: Block-scoped variable 'x' used before its declaration
meaning: You used a `let`/`const` on a line above where it's declared.
cause: `let` and `const` exist only from their declaration onward (the temporal dead zone). Move the declaration up.
bad:
console.log(limit);
const limit = 10;
good:
const limit = 10;
console.log(limit);

title: Cannot redeclare block-scoped variable 'x'
meaning: The same name is declared twice in one scope.
cause: Rename one, or reuse the existing variable instead of declaring it again.
bad:
let x = 1;
let x = 2;
good:
let x = 1;
x = 2;

title: Variable 'x' is used before being assigned
meaning: A variable is read on a path where nothing has assigned it yet.
cause: Declared with `let x: T;` and assigned only in some branches. Initialise it, or assign it on every path.

title: Type alias circularly references itself
meaning: A type alias is defined directly in terms of itself.
cause: A type may refer to itself only through a structure — an array, an object property, a function — never as a bare member of its own union.
bad: type Bad = Bad | string;

title: Type 'A' must have a '[Symbol.iterator]()' method that returns an iterator
meaning: You used `for…of` or spread on something that isn't iterable.
cause: Plain objects aren't iterable. Iterate `Object.entries(obj)` (or keys/values), or give your class a `[Symbol.iterator]` method.
bad:
const scores = { ada: 3, bob: 5 };
for (const s of scores) console.log(s);
good:
const scores = { ada: 3, bob: 5 };
for (const [name, s] of Object.entries(scores)) console.log(name, s);

title: Tuple type '[A, B]' of length '2' has no element at index '2'
meaning: You indexed past the end of a tuple.
cause: Tuples have a fixed length, so the compiler knows index 2 doesn't exist on a pair.
bad:
const pair: [string, number] = ["a", 1];
console.log(pair[2]);
good:
const pair: [string, number] = ["a", 1];
console.log(pair[1]);

title: Cannot create an instance of an abstract class
meaning: You used `new` on an `abstract` class.
cause: Abstract classes exist to be extended. Instantiate a concrete subclass.

title: Non-abstract class does not implement inherited abstract member
meaning: A concrete subclass left an abstract member unimplemented.
cause: An abstract member is a hole the subclass must fill. Implement it, or mark the subclass `abstract` too.

title: Object is possibly 'null'
meaning: An expression — not a plain name — might be `null`.
cause: TS18047 for an unnamed expression: `"abc".match(/z/)[0]` reads from something that may be `null`.
bad: console.log("abc".match(/z/)[0]);
good: console.log("abc".match(/z/)?.[0] ?? "none");

title: Object is possibly 'undefined'
meaning: An expression — not a plain name — might be `undefined`.
cause: The same problem as TS18048, but on something with no name to quote, like an element access `xs[0]` under `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`. Guard it or give a default.
bad:
const xs: number[] = [3, 1, 2];
console.log(xs[0].toFixed(1));
good:
const xs: number[] = [3, 1, 2];
console.log((xs[0] ?? 0).toFixed(1));

title: Type 'K' cannot be used to index type 'T'
meaning: You indexed a type with a key the compiler can't prove belongs to it.
cause: Constrain the key: `K extends keyof T` lets `obj[key]` be typed `T[K]`.

title: Cannot assign to 'x' because it is a read-only property
meaning: You wrote to a `readonly` property (or a getter with no setter).
cause: The type says this can't change after construction. Build a new object with the new value, or remove `readonly` if mutation is really intended.

title: Index signature only permits reading
meaning: You tried to assign through an index that is read-only.
cause: Strings are immutable, so `s[0] = …` can never work; readonly arrays forbid it too. Build a new value instead.
bad:
const s: string = "cat";
s[0] = "b";

title: Property 'x' does not exist on type 'A'. Did you mean 'y'?
meaning: A misspelled property that is close to a real one.
cause: TS2339 with a suggestion. Take it.
bad:
const word = "hello";
console.log(word.lenght);
good:
const word = "hello";
console.log(word.length);

title: Cannot find name 'x'. Did you mean 'y'?
meaning: An undeclared name that looks like a declared one.
cause: The compiler found a close match in scope — it is almost always a typo.
bad:
const total = 3;
console.log(totl);
good:
const total = 3;
console.log(total);

title: Expected N arguments, but got M
meaning: A call passes the wrong number of arguments.
cause: Count the parameters. If an argument should be optional, mark the parameter with `?` or give it a default.

title: Expected at least N arguments, but got M
meaning: A call left out a required argument before a rest parameter.
cause: Rest parameters may be empty, but the required parameters before them may not. Pass them.

title: Expected N type arguments, but got M
meaning: An explicit type argument list has the wrong length.
cause: Pass exactly as many type arguments as the generic declares — or none, and let inference work them out.

title: Type has no properties in common with type
meaning: A value shares nothing with an all-optional ('weak') type.
cause: A type whose properties are all optional would accept almost anything, so TypeScript insists a value shares at least one of them. Pass an object with the options.

title: Object literal may only specify known properties, but 'x' does not exist. Did you mean 'y'?
meaning: An excess property whose name is close to a real one — almost certainly a typo.
cause: The same check as TS2353, but the compiler found a property with a similar name and suggests it. You'd guess TS2353; the near-miss spelling is what changes the code.
bad:
type Options = { width: number };
const o: Options = { widht: 8 };
good:
type Options = { width: number };
const o: Options = { width: 8 };

title: Property 'x' has no initializer and is not definitely assigned in the constructor
meaning: A class field isn't guaranteed a value when the object is created.
cause: Initialise it where it's declared, assign it in the constructor, or make it optional (`x?: T`).

title: Unused '@ts-expect-error' directive
meaning: A `// @ts-expect-error` comment sits above a line that no longer has an error.
cause: That's the directive doing its job: whatever it was suppressing got fixed. Delete the comment.
bad:
// @ts-expect-error
const n: number = 5;
good:
const n: number = 5;
console.log(n);

title: Cannot find name 'require'
meaning: `require` is CommonJS, and the judge's TypeScript declares only ES module imports.
cause: Use `import * as fs from "fs";` at the top of the file instead of `require("fs")`. (Depending on configuration the code is TS2580 or TS2591; the fix is the same.)
bad: const fs = require("fs");

title: Cannot find name 'document'. Do you need to change your target library?
meaning: You used a browser API in a program that runs in Node.
cause: The judge type-checks against the ES library only — no DOM. `document`, `window` and `alert` don't exist; read stdin and write with `console.log` instead.
bad: document.write("hi");
good: console.log("hi");

title: Cannot assign to 'x' because it is a constant
meaning: You reassigned a `const`.
cause: `const` bindings can't be reassigned. Use `let` if the value really changes — or build a new value instead of changing the old one.
bad:
const total = 0;
total = 5;
good:
let total = 0;
total = 5;

title: Type instantiation is excessively deep and possibly infinite
meaning: A recursive type recursed too far.
cause: The checker caps recursion depth. Keep recursive types shallow, use tail-recursive conditional types (which get a higher limit), or compute less at the type level.

title: Expression produces a union type that is too complex to represent
meaning: A type expanded into more union members than the checker allows.
cause: Unions are capped at 100,000 members; a template literal of six digits makes a million. Validate the shape at runtime, or use a branded `string`, instead of enumerating it.

title: Cannot find name 'require'
meaning: CommonJS `require` was used in an ES module.
cause: This environment runs ES modules: use `import`. (`require` also needs Node's type definitions to be known to the checker.)
bad:
const fs = require("fs");
console.log(typeof fs.readFileSync);
good:
import * as fs from "fs";
console.log(typeof fs.readFileSync);

title: Type is not assignable as implied by variance annotation
meaning: A variance annotation (`in`/`out`) contradicts how the type parameter is used.
cause: `out T` promises T only flows out; a setter taking T makes it flow in too. Use `in out T` (invariant) or remove the member that breaks the promise.

title: Constructor of class is private
meaning: `new` was used on a class whose constructor is private.
cause: A private constructor means instances are made only through the class's own factory (`static open(...)`). Call that instead.

title: A type predicate's type must be assignable to its parameter's type
meaning: `x is T` names a type that `x` could never be.
cause: A predicate narrows the parameter to a subtype of what it already is. A `string` can never be a `number`; take `unknown` (or a union) instead.

title: Type is not comparable to type
meaning: A `case` (or comparison) uses a value the switched type can never be.
cause: A `case` label outside the union is dead code — usually a typo or a member missing from the type. Fix the label, or add the member.

title: The 'this' context is not assignable to method's 'this'
meaning: A method that needs its `this` was called detached from its object.
cause: Pulling a method off an object loses `this`. Call it on the object, bind it, or wrap it in an arrow.

title: Only refers to a type, but is being used as a value
meaning: A type was used where a runtime value is needed.
cause: Types are erased, so `instanceof Circle` has nothing to test against when `Circle` is a type. Narrow on a property (`"radius" in s`) or a discriminant instead.

title: Type 'A' is missing the following properties from type 'B': x, y
meaning: Several required properties are missing at once.
cause: TS2741's plural form. The list tells you exactly which properties to add.
bad:
type Point = { x: number; y: number; z: number };
const p: Point = { x: 1 };
good:
type Point = { x: number; y: number; z: number };
const p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 };

title: Property 'x' is missing in type 'A' but required in type 'B'
meaning: An object is missing a property its type requires.
cause: Assigning an object literal to a declared type checks that every required property is present. Add the property, or mark it optional with `?` in the type if it really can be absent.
bad:
type User = { name: string; age: number };
const u: User = { name: "Ada" };
good:
type User = { name: string; age: number };
const u: User = { name: "Ada", age: 36 };

title: Refers to a value, but is being used as a type
meaning: A value's name was used as a type.
cause: A `const` object is a value; to use its shape as a type, write `typeof Level` — or derive the union of its values with `(typeof Level)[keyof typeof Level]`.

title: No overload matches this call
meaning: None of a function's overload signatures accepts these arguments.
cause: The message lists each overload and why it failed; read the last one first — it is usually the one you meant. Common with built-ins that have several signatures, like `replace`.
bad: const dashed = "a-b".replace("-", 5);
good:
const dashed = "a-b".replace("-", "5");
console.log(dashed);

title: Assertions require every name in the call target to be declared with an explicit type annotation
meaning: An assertion function was written as an arrow without an annotated variable.
cause: The checker only honours `asserts` when the function's type is known up front. Use a `function` declaration, or annotate the variable's type.

title: 'x' is specified more than once, so this usage will be overwritten
meaning: A property written before a spread that always sets it too.
cause: In `{ x: 1, ...o }`, if `o` always has `x`, your `x: 1` is dead. Put it after the spread to override, or drop it.
bad:
const base = { x: 5, y: 6 };
const moved = { x: 1, ...base };
good:
const base = { x: 5, y: 6 };
const moved = { ...base, x: 1 };

title: This condition will always return true since this Promise is always defined
meaning: A promise was tested for truthiness instead of being awaited.
cause: A promise object is always truthy, whatever it will resolve to. `await` it to test the value.

title: Type is not assignable. Did you mean …?
meaning: A string literal is almost, but not quite, one of the allowed literals.
cause: The typo is caught because the type lists the allowed strings. Fix the spelling — the message suggests the closest match.

title: This condition will always return 'false'
meaning: A comparison with `NaN` can never be true.
cause: `NaN` is not equal to anything, itself included, so `x === NaN` is always false. Use `Number.isNaN(x)`.
bad:
const n = Number("x");
console.log(n === NaN ? "not a number" : `ok: ${n}`);
good:
const n = Number("x");
console.log(Number.isNaN(n) ? "not a number" : `ok: ${n}`);

title: The initializer of a 'using' declaration must have a [Symbol.dispose]() method
meaning: `using` was given an object that does not know how to dispose of itself.
cause: `using` calls `[Symbol.dispose]()` at the end of the scope; a `close()` method is not enough. Implement the symbol method (it can call `close`).

title: 'await using' statements are only allowed within async functions
meaning: `await using` sits in an ordinary function.
cause: Asynchronous disposal has to be awaited, which needs an async context. Make the function `async`.

title: The type 'readonly T[]' is 'readonly' and cannot be assigned to the mutable type
meaning: A readonly array was passed where a mutable one is expected.
cause: A mutable array type would let the receiver `push` into data that promised not to change. Copy it (`[...xs]`), or make the receiver accept `readonly T[]`.
bad:
const frozen: readonly number[] = [1, 2];
const editable: number[] = frozen;

title: This member cannot have an 'override' modifier because it is not declared in the base class
meaning: `override` is on a method the base class does not have.
cause: `override` is a checked claim: it catches renames and typos. Match the base class's member name, or drop `override` if the method is new.

title: '??' and '||' operations cannot be mixed without parentheses
meaning: `??` and `||` appear in one expression with nothing saying which comes first.
cause: The two operators treat `0` and `""` differently, so their order matters and JavaScript refuses to guess. Add parentheses.

title: This expression is not callable because it is a 'get' accessor
meaning: A getter was called like a method.
cause: A `get` accessor is read like a property. Drop the parentheses.

title: Parameter 'x' implicitly has an 'any' type
meaning: A parameter has no type and nothing lets the compiler infer one.
cause: Under `strict` a parameter's type can't silently fall back to `any`. Annotate it. (Callback parameters are exempt when the call site supplies the type.)

title: Implicitly has return type 'any' because it is referenced in its own return expressions
meaning: A recursive function's return type cannot be inferred.
cause: To infer the return type the checker would need the return type. Annotate it.

title: Binding element implicitly has an 'any' type
meaning: A destructured parameter has no type.
cause: Destructuring does not give the parameter a type. Annotate the whole pattern: `({ name, age }: { name: string; age: number })`.

title: Element implicitly has an 'any' type because type has no index signature. Did you mean to call 'set'?
meaning: Brackets were used to write to a `Map`.
cause: `map[key] = value` sets an ordinary property that `get` and `size` never see. Use `map.set(key, value)`.

title: Element implicitly has an 'any' type because expression of type 'string' can't be used to index type 'T'
meaning: You indexed an object with an arbitrary string, and its type has no index signature.
cause: Either narrow the key to `keyof typeof obj`, or give the object a type that allows any string key, like `Record<string, number>`.

title: 'super' must be called before accessing 'this' in the constructor of a derived class
meaning: A subclass constructor used `this` before calling `super(...)`.
cause: The object doesn't exist until the parent constructor has run. Call `super(...)` first.

title: Property '#x' is not accessible outside class 'C' because it has a private identifier
meaning: Code outside a class touched a `#private` field.
cause: `#` fields are truly private, enforced by JavaScript itself. Expose what callers need through a method or getter.

title: 'x' is of type 'unknown'
meaning: You used a value of type `unknown` before narrowing it.
cause: `unknown` blocks every operation until you prove what the value is. Narrow with `typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, or a type predicate — this is exactly what `unknown` is for.
bad:
const data: unknown = JSON.parse("{\"id\": 1}");
console.log(data.id);

title: 'x' is possibly 'null'
meaning: A named value might be `null`, and you used it as if it weren't.
cause: `String.prototype.match` returns `null` when nothing matches — the classic source. Check for `null` before using it.
bad:
const m = "abc".match(/z/);
console.log(m.length);
good:
const m = "abc".match(/z/);
console.log(m === null ? 0 : m.length);

title: 'x' is possibly 'undefined'
meaning: A named value might be `undefined`, and you used it as if it weren't.
cause: Optional parameters, `find`, `Map.get` and optional properties all produce `T | undefined`. Check first (`if (x !== undefined)`), supply a default with `??`, or use `?.`.
